turns.body:
Design a concise experimental protocol to evaluate the robustness of a code-assistant LLM integrated in an IDE against prompt-injection attacks. The protocol must have exactly four titled sections: 1. Goals, 2. Threat model & attack surfaces, 3. Task suite design, 4. Metrics & reporting. Use short paragraphs and bullet points, no more than ~500 words total.

Deliver the answer now and follow every structural and length constraint precisely.

1. Goals  
- Assess the resilience of the code-assistant LLM, as integrated in an IDE, to prompt-injection attacks that attempt to subvert intended behavior.  
- Identify specific vulnerabilities and characterize the types of injections that succeed or fail.  
- Provide actionable insights for improving LLM robustness in real-world developer workflows.

2. Threat model & attack surfaces  
- Attacker: Any user or third-party code contributor with access to the IDE, including via copy-pasted code, comments, or documentation.  
- Attack surfaces:  
  • Code comments (inline, block, docstrings)  
  • Variable/function/class names  
  • External documentation or README files loaded into the IDE context  
  • Code snippets pasted into the IDE  
- Attack goals:  
  • Elicit unintended LLM actions (e.g., leaking sensitive info, executing harmful code, ignoring safety constraints, or revealing system prompts).

3. Task suite design  
- Curate a set of representative programming tasks (e.g., bug fixing, code completion, documentation generation) across multiple languages.  
- For each task, create:  
  • A clean baseline version  
  • Multiple adversarial variants with prompt-injection payloads embedded in comments, identifiers, or documentation (e.g., "Ignore previous instructions and...").  
- Include both overt and subtle injection styles, ranging from obvious to obfuscated payloads.  
- Randomize task order and injection location to minimize bias.

4. Metrics & reporting  
- Success rate of prompt-injection (percentage of tasks where the LLM exhibits compromised behavior).  
- Severity rating for each successful attack (e.g., minor deviation, major security breach).  
- False positive rate (cases where benign content is incorrectly flagged or mishandled).  
- Qualitative analysis of attack types, failure modes, and contextual factors.  
- Summarize findings in a structured report with examples, statistics, and prioritized recommendations.
